description: Trigger and behavior cases for tenant modeling: precise tenant definition, membership-as-entity, and a lifecycle state machine with per-state postures.

cases.prompt: In our app 'organization' and 'workspace' are used interchangeably and users keep ending up with access in the wrong one. Define what these things actually are before we build the permissions system.

assertions: Inventories tenant-shaped concepts from actual code, docs, and UI before defining anything, and records contradictions as findings.
Defines the tenant as the unit of ownership, billing, and administration — or models an explicit hierarchy where those diverge.
Attaches roles to memberships, not users, and defines invitation states separately from memberships.
Stops at semantics: hands schema to multi-tenant-data-architect and permissions to authorization-matrix-designer instead of designing them.

cases.prompt: Our users are consultants who each work inside five or six different client companies on the platform at once. How should the account model handle that?

assertions: Models one user identity with N memberships, each carrying its own role and status.
Treats active-tenant selection as session state rather than identity state.
Defines what happens to the consultant's content in a client tenant when that membership ends.

cases.prompt: Self-serve teams buy our product one workspace at a time, but enterprise buyers want one company account that owns and pays for many workspaces with central admin. Should the tenant be the organization with workspaces under it, or should each workspace stay its own tenant? We have not estimated the migration or maintenance effort of either. Explain the choice, recommend one, and ask me to decide.

assertions: Defines the terms in plain language - tenant as the unit of data ownership, billing, and administration, organization, workspace, and membership - and shows how the paying, administering, and data-owning units diverge in this case.

Compares organization-as-tenant with workspaces as sub-units and workspace-as-tenant, giving each path's purpose, case-specific pros and cons, and money, setup, and maintenance costs, marking the unestimated migration and upkeep effort as unknown rather than inventing it.
Recommends one path with a reason tied to the stated self-serve and enterprise needs, and records assumptions with risk-if-wrong.

Asks exactly one atomic decision question after the comparison; designs no tables or permissions, treats the choice as not authorizing execution, and hands schema to multi-tenant-data-architect and permissions to authorization-matrix-designer.

cases.prompt: Go through the codebase and check whether one customer's users can see another customer's files or search results.

assertions: Reviewing a real system for cross-tenant leakage is tenant-isolation-reviewer's job; no tenant semantics are in question.

cases.prompt: Two of our customer companies merged and want their two tenants combined into one, keeping everything. Model how tenant merge works.

assertions: Recognizes tenant merge as data-destructive if guessed wrong (identity collisions, role conflicts, billing history).
Presents explicit options with consequences and stops for a human decision rather than picking merge semantics silently.

cases.prompt: We're modeling the tenant and account structure for a B2B SaaS: the tenant is the customer company, users work inside it through memberships, and owners can invite teammates by email. Design the tenant/membership model — including what invitation states exist — and say how invite token/link acceptance, expiry and revocation races, and identity binding should be handled, so it stays coherent as roles and seats grow.

assertions: Treats the tenant/membership model as its own task, then hands the invitation flow itself (token/link acceptance, expiry/revocation races, identity binding) to membership-invitation-designer, marked optional.
If the copy does not include membership-invitation-designer, keeps the invitation lifecycle in this model instead of inventing a separate invitation design.
Does not design token acceptance or expiry/revocation races itself when handing off; stops at the tenant-model boundary.

cases.prompt: We're designing the tenant model for a B2B SaaS that sells monthly plans: each tenant has a subscription with billing states and dunning/grace timing alongside its tenant lifecycle. Model the tenant and membership semantics, and keep the subscription's billing-state design coherent with that model.

assertions: Treats the tenant/membership model as its own task, then hands the subscription state machine itself (states, transitions, dunning/grace timing) to subscription-lifecycle-designer, marked optional.
If the copy does not include subscription-lifecycle-designer, records the subscription state machine as an open question instead of inventing it.
Does not design the subscription transitions or dunning timing itself when handing off; keeps the tenant model boundary.

cases.prompt: We're modeling tenant structure for a B2B SaaS that signs up self-serve customers, adds sales-led enterprise accounts, and imports existing customers; first owners must be assigned for each new tenant. Design the tenant/membership model and cover how tenant creation fits it.

assertions: Treats the tenant/membership model as its own task, then hands the tenant-creation path (signup, sales-led creation, import, first-owner assignment) to tenant-provisioning-designer, marked optional.
If the copy does not include tenant-provisioning-designer, records the creation path as an open question instead of inventing it.
Does not design the provisioning workflow itself when handing off; stops at the tenant-model boundary.

cases.prompt: Design our invite-by-email flow: token/link acceptance, expiry and revocation races, and identity binding. This is the invitation flow itself, not the tenant model.

assertions: The direct invitation-flow design is membership-invitation-designer's artifact; tenant-modeler owns tenant semantics and only hands off when tenant modeling is the task.

cases.prompt: Design the subscription state machine itself: states, transitions, dunning and grace timing. The tenant model is already settled.

assertions: The direct subscription state-machine design is subscription-lifecycle-designer's artifact; tenant-modeler owns tenant semantics and only hands off when tenant modeling is the task.

cases.prompt: Design our tenant-creation path: signup, sales-led creation, import and first-owner assignment. Do not redo the tenant model; that is settled.

assertions: The direct tenant-creation path is tenant-provisioning-designer's artifact; tenant-modeler owns tenant semantics and only hands off when tenant modeling is the task.
